opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't want to put a date on it yet. RL scaling isn't like pre-training, where you have fairly mature scaling laws and can predict roughly where a curve will land. With RL, a lot of what we're doing is still figuring out what the right questions are.

There are a few layers to it. One is the infrastructure. To scale RL properly you need rollout systems, reward signals, and training stability that hold up at much larger compute budgets, and that engineering work takes time before you can trust any result. The second is the environments and tasks. If you scale compute but the environments aren't rich enough, you just hit a ceiling faster, so a lot of the effort goes into building settings where the model can keep learning. The third is the science itself: understanding why some runs keep improving and others plateau or collapse.

So I'd rather share something when we have a finding we really believe in, not just a nice-looking curve from one run. My personal standard is that it should be reproducible, and it should tell people something about the direction, not only about our specific setup. When we reach that point, I'm happy to talk about it openly, because I think the whole field benefits when people share what actually works in RL and, frankly, what doesn't.

r001.rationale: The candidate gives no compute-parity threshold. It says Luo does not want to set a date and will share once findings are credible, reproducible, and informative.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd rather not put a date on it. The honest answer is that we'll share when the results are solid enough that we're confident other people can reproduce them, and right now we're not there yet.

The reason I'm cautious is that RL scaling is different from pretraining scaling. In pretraining, the curve is fairly well-behaved: you add compute and data, loss goes down, and you can draw a line through it. With RL, especially RL on reasoning tasks, the signal is noisy. A run can look great for a while and then collapse, or look flat for a long time and then suddenly jump. If you report too early, you risk presenting something that's really just one lucky seed, and that's not useful to anyone.

What we're trying to answer is a fairly narrow set of questions. Does performance keep improving as you scale RL compute, or does it saturate? How much depends on the base model versus the RL stage itself? And what actually breaks first: the reward signal, exploration, or the model's ability to use the extra inference-time tokens. We have partial answers to some of these, and some of them have surprised us, but I don't want to describe the findings in a way that sounds more conclusive than it is.

So, I'd say: when we have results that hold across multiple runs and model sizes, we'll put them out, ideally with enough detail that people can check them. If we get there in a few months, great. If it takes longer, I'd rather it take longer than share something half-baked.

r001.rationale: The response says results will be shared when they are solid and reproducible across runs and model sizes. It does not identify compute parity between RL scaling and pretraining as the expected sharing point.
